source_text:
Et Octauius: Dicam equidem, ut potero pro uiribus, et adnitendum tibi mecum est, ut conuiciorum amarissimam labem uerborum ueracium flumine diluamusnec dissimulabo principio ita Natalis mei errantem, uagam, lubricam nutasse sententiam, ut sit nobis ambigendum, utrum uersutia turbata sit, an uacillauerit per errorem.
nam mcerim aeos creaere, mteum se aeliberare uariauit, ut propositionis incerto incertior responsionis nostrae intentio fundaretur. sed in Natali meo uersutiam nolo, non credo: procul est ab eius simplicitate subtilis urbanitas. quid igitur?
ut qui rectam uiam nescit, ubi, ut fit, in plures una cliffinditur, [quia uiam nescit] haeret anxius nec singulas audet eligere nec uniuersas probare: sic cui non est ueri stabile iudicium, prout infida suspicio spargitur.
ita eius dubia opinio dissipatur. nullum itaque miraculum est, si Caecilius identidem in contrariis ac repugnantibus iactetur, aestuet, fluctuetur. quod ne fiat ulterius, conuincam et redarguam. quamuis sint diuersa quae dicta sunt, una ueritate confirmata probataque nec dubitandum ei de cetero est nec uagandum.
et quoniam mens frater erupit, aegre se ferre, stomachari, indignari, dolere, inliteratos, pauperes, inperitos de rebus caelestibus disputare, sciat omnes homines sine dilectu aetatis, sexus, dignitatis rationis et sensus capaces et habiles procreatos nec fortuna nanctos, sed natura insitos esse sapientiam: quin. ipsos etiam philosophos, uel si qui alii artium repertores in memorias exierunt, priusquam sollertia mentis parerent nominis claritatem, habitos esse plebeios, indoctos, seminudos: adeo diuites facultatibus suis inligatos magis aurum suspicere consuesse quam caelum, nostrates pauperes et commentos esse prudentiam et tradidisse ceteris disciplinam. unde apparet ingenium non dari facultatibus nec studio parari, sed cum ipsa mentis formatione generari.
nihil itaque indignandum uel dolendum, si quicumque de diuinis quaerat, quae sentiat proferat, cum non disputantis auctoritas, sed disputationis ipsius ueritas requiratur. atque etiam, quo imperitior sermo, hoc inlustrior ratio est, quoniam non fucatur pompa facundiae et gratiae, sed, ut est, recti regula sustinetur.
thought_title: Octavius opens his reply: truth, not eloquence, must settle the debate
orientation: Octavius, the Christian friend, begins his reply to Caecilius's attack on Christianity, addressing the narrator Marcus and the assembled friends.
pass_a_gloss: And Octavius said: I will speak indeed, as I shall be able, according to my strength, and you must strive together with me, so that we may wash away the very bitter stain of insults with a stream of truthful words. Nor will I conceal at the beginning that the opinion of my Natalis has wavered so erring, wandering, slippery, that we must be uncertain whether it has been disturbed by cunning, or whether it has tottered through error. For now he has varied between believing the gods and freeing himself from them, so that by the uncertainty of his proposition a more uncertain foundation of our response might be laid. But in my Natalis I do not want cunning, I do not believe it: subtle urbanity is far from his simplicity. What then? As he who does not know the straight way, where, as happens, one way is split into several, because he does not know the way, sticks anxiously and dares neither to choose the single ones nor to approve all of them: so he for whom there is no stable judgment of truth, insofar as unfaithful suspicion is scattered. Thus his doubtful opinion is dispersed. Therefore it is no wonder, if Caecilius is repeatedly tossed about in contrary and conflicting things, burns, fluctuates. So that this may not happen further, I will refute and disprove. Although the things which have been said are diverse, once the one truth has been confirmed and proved, he must neither doubt about the rest nor wander. And since my brother's mind has burst out, that he bears it badly, is angry, is indignant, grieves, that unlettered, poor, inexperienced people dispute about heavenly things, let him know that all human beings, without distinction of age, sex, dignity, have been created capable and fit of reason and sense, and that wisdom has not been obtained by fortune, but implanted by nature: indeed even the philosophers themselves, or if any other discoverers of arts have gone out into memories, before their skill of mind produced the brightness of their name, were considered common, untaught, half-naked: so much so that the rich, entangled in their own resources, have been accustomed to admire gold more than heaven, while our poor people have both devised wisdom and handed down discipline to the rest. Whence it appears that talent is not given by resources nor acquired by study, but is generated with the very formation of the mind. Therefore nothing is to be resented or grieved, if whoever inquires about divine things brings forth what he thinks, since not the authority of the disputant, but the truth of the disputation itself is required. And even, the more unskilled the speech, the more illustrious the reason is, since it is not colored by the pomp of eloquence and charm, but, as it is, is sustained by the rule of right.

choices.term: conuiciorum amarissimam labem uerborum ueracium flumine diluamus
choices.english: wash away the very bitter stain of insults with a stream of truthful words
choices.why: Keeps the metaphor of washing away a stain with a stream, preserving the contrast between insults and truthful words.
rejected: cleanse the bitter stain of insults with a river of true words

choices.why: Preserves the verb of wavering, which is central to Octavius's claim that Caecilius's position is unstable.

choices.term: uersutia turbata sit, an uacillauerit per errorem
choices.english: whether it has been disturbed by cunning, or whether it has tottered through error
choices.why: Keeps the two alternatives distinct: deliberate cunning versus accidental error.
rejected: whether it was upset by trickery or stumbled by mistake

choices.term: procul est ab eius simplicitate subtilis urbanitas
choices.english: subtle urbanity is far from his simplicity
choices.why: Preserves the abstract nouns and the spatial metaphor of distance.
rejected: his simple nature is far from subtle wit

choices.term: nec fortuna nanctos, sed natura insitos esse sapientiam
choices.english: wisdom has not been obtained by fortune, but implanted by nature
choices.why: Keeps the contrast between fortune and nature, and the passive sense of wisdom being implanted.
rejected: wisdom is not gotten by luck but inborn by nature

choices.term: non fucatur pompa facundiae et gratiae
choices.english: it is not colored by the pomp of eloquence and charm
choices.why: Preserves the metaphor of cosmetic coloring, which contrasts with the plain truth.
rejected: it is not painted over with the show of eloquence and grace

pass_b_english: Octavius replied: "I will speak as best I can, and you must strive with me to wash away the bitter stain of insults with a stream of truthful words. I will not conceal at the outset that my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered, wandering and slippery, so that we must ask whether it has been disturbed by cunning, or whether it has tottered through error. For he has varied between believing in the gods and freeing himself from fear, so that by the uncertainty of his proposition the intention of our response might be founded on even less certainty. But I do not want to see cunning in my Natalis, and I do not believe it: subtle urbanity is far from his simplicity. What then? As a man who does not know the right way, when, as happens, one road splits into several, because he does not know the way, sticks anxiously and dares neither to choose each one nor to approve them all: so it is with a man who has no stable judgment of truth, as unreliable suspicion scatters. Thus his doubtful opinion is dispersed. It is no wonder, then, if Caecilius is repeatedly tossed among contrary and conflicting positions, seething and wavering. To prevent this from happening any further, I will refute and disprove him. Although the things that have been said are diverse, once the one truth has been confirmed and proved, he must neither doubt nor wander any longer.

And since my brother's mind has burst out, saying that he is aggrieved, angry, indignant, and pained that uneducated, poor, and inexperienced people should debate about heavenly matters, let him know that all human beings, without distinction of age, sex, or rank, have been created capable and fit for reason and perception, and that wisdom has not been obtained by fortune, but implanted by nature. Indeed, even the philosophers themselves, or any others who have gone down in memory as discoverers of arts, before their mental skill produced the brilliance of their names, were considered common, untaught, half-naked: so true is it that the rich, entangled in their own resources, are accustomed to admire gold more than heaven, while our poor people have both devised wisdom and handed down learning to others. From this it is clear that talent is not given by wealth nor acquired by study, but is generated with the very formation of the mind.

So no one should be indignant or pained if anyone inquires about divine things and brings forward what he thinks, since what is required is not the authority of the speaker, but the truth of the argument itself. And indeed, the more unpolished the speech, the more brilliant the reason, because it is not colored by the pomp of eloquence and charm, but, as it is, is upheld by the rule of what is right."
notes: The source text contains 'mcerim aeos creaere, mteum se aeliberare uariauit', which appears to be OCR damage. The likely reading is 'modo deos credere, modo se deliberare uariauit' or similar, meaning 'now he has varied between believing the gods and freeing himself from them'. The gloss reflects this probable reading, but the exact wording is uncertain.
The source text contains 'cliffinditur', which appears to be a misspelling or OCR error for 'diffinditur' (from diffindo, to split).

last_rejected.why: Source is corrupt but likely reads 'nam meritos eos credere, mentem se liberare'; 'meritos' not rendered.
last_rejected.fix: For he has varied between believing them deserved and freeing his mind
last_rejected.ruling: Source line is corrupted; 'meritos' uncertain, translation plausible; omission is minor nuance, not a major meaning change.
